hints: Look closely at what happens to the carbon-carbon double bond in ethene when it becomes ethanol.
Notice that ethene, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$, is unsaturated while ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, is saturated, so H and OH have joined across the double bond.
Think about which reaction type combines two reactant molecules completely into one single product with nothing swapped out or split off.
walkthrough:
**See what changes in the organic molecule**

Ethene has a C=C double bond. Ethanol has only C-C single bonds with an extra H and OH added on.

Chemical change:
$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Recall what addition means**

In addition, two molecules combine to make one bigger molecule. The pi bond of the alkene breaks and the atoms from the small molecule join to the two carbons.

General idea for alkenes:
$$\text{C=C} + \text{X-Y} \rightarrow \text{X-C-C-Y}$$

**Check against the other types**

Here $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ adds as H and OH across the double bond. Nothing is replaced and nothing is split apart by water, and there is no neutralisation. That is the classic electrophilic addition of steam to make an alcohol.

options.A: Not acid-base. Sulfuric acid is only a catalyst here, it is not neutralised by a base. The trap is seeing the word acid and assuming neutralisation must be happening.
options.B: Correct. Water adds across the C=C double bond of ethene to give ethanol. Two reactants combine into one product with the pi bond broken, which is electrophilic addition.
options.C: Not hydrolysis. Hydrolysis uses water to split a molecule into two smaller pieces, such as an ester into acid and alcohol. Here water is used to build up, joining to ethene to make one larger molecule.
options.D: Not substitution. Substitution swaps one atom or group for another, with something removed. Here nothing leaves ethene, H and OH are simply added across the double bond.
